newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Premier says Burundi not to blame for massacres.
newsitem.headline: Premier says Burundi not to blame for massacres.

text.p: Burundi's prime minister said on Friday his government had no responsibility for incidents like the reported massacre of 300 Hutu refugees in the troubled northwestern Cibitoke region.

Pascal Firmin Ndimira was asked about the incident at a news conference in Stockholm, where he had called on Swedish Foreign Minister Lena Hjelm-Wallen as part of a European campaign to urge the lifting of sanctions against Burundi.
The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR on Friday reported the Cibitoke massacre and said it had happened a month ago when the refugees were on their way from Zaire.
The Hutus were killed in a church in Murambi village in Cibitoke, where Hutu rebels and Burundi's almost exclusively Tutsi army are fighting a guerrilla war, a UNHCR spokeswoman said.
They were among some 3,000 Burundian Hutus who fled a Tutsi revolt in east Zaire and crossed to Cibitoke.
UNHCR announced the massacre a day after the London-based human rights group Amnesty International reported it.

"The government has no responsibility for this killing. It is non-uniformed rebels who would have done that," Ndimira said, adding that the United Nations and aid organisations were not always correctly informed.
"The Burundi army's most important task is to separate rebels from innocent civilians," Ndimira said.
Ndimira described the greatest danger facing his country as "the culture of genocide", reflecting years of violence between Hutus and Tutsis there and in neighbouring Rwanda.

Burundi's neighbours imposed an economic embargo on the African state and the European Parliament urged European Union member states to refuse to recognise Major Pierre Buyoya's new regime which seized power in a July coup.

In a non-binding resolution approved in September, the European Parliament urged an extension of the ban on weapons and ammunition to put further pressure on the Burundi leadership to restore democracy.
Ndimira, who also called on Cabinet Secretary Jan Eliasson in Stockholm, was expected to have urged Sweden to use its influence with Tanzania to bring about a lifting of sanctions.
The economic blockade had prevented the export of tens of thousands of tonnes of tea and coffee and the import of pharmaceuticals and fertilisers, he said.
"We cannot take part in peace talks in Arusha, Tanzania before sanctions are lifted," Ndimira said.
